Abdollahi had previously led the Khatam al-Anbiya, Iran's inter-branch central military command tasked with coordinating operations. A statement on Khamenei's website announced that "Major General Ali Abdollahi has been appointed chief of staff of the armed forces. Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi has also been appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps with the rank of major general." The pair represent Khamenei's first senior military appointments since being named supreme leader early in the Middle East war after the death of his father in US-Israeli strikes.

items.summary: Iran sets conditions for reopening Strait of Hormuz Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has outlined Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB, Zolghadr said Washington must “correct its behaviour” by: Ending threats against Iran and its “sacred values” Permanently halting military action against Iran and its regional allies Withdrawing US naval and air forces involved in the blockade of Iran Compensating Iran for damage inflicted during the recent conflict Lifting US sanctions Releasing frozen Iranian assets “The Supreme National Security Council will not retreat from these demands, whether in war or in negotiations,” Zolghadr said.

clusters.headline: Why the Trump administration will have to accept a Hormuz toll

items.title: Why the Trump administration will have to accept a Hormuz toll
items.summary: In the weeks since the U.S.-Iran Memorandum of Understanding collapsed, Washington and Tehran have used the time to strengthen their respective positions in the event negotiations resume. For the United States, this has largely taken the form of overt threats by President Donald Trump himself and hints that an even more comprehensive U.S. bombing campaign against Iranian strategic targets is on the table. For Iran, the strategy is familiar: ensure maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is kept to an absolute minimum . U.S. and Iranian officials continue to give conflicting accounts of where negotiations stand. Despite Trump’s repeated declarations that Tehran is begging for a deal, the Iranians stress no talks are occurring with the United States. Still, both sides seem to agree that any pending agreement will center on the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has proved capable of shutting down at will. items.summary: Trump could declare victory if Iran reopens Strait of Hormuz: Report US President Donald Trump is prepared to declare victory in the war with Iran if Tehran restores shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, according to The Wall Street Journal. US officials told the newspaper that Trump has privately indicated he could abandon efforts to secure a nuclear agreement with Iran in return for reopening the strategic waterway. Trump is reportedly willing to let negotiations continue, particularly while petrol prices in the US remain stable. A White House official said Washington had achieved its military objectives in Iran and that Trump was now prioritising the movement of oil through the strait. The US would maintain forces in the region and could attack Iran again if Tehran targeted vessels, the report added. Trump also believes Iran cannot rebuild its nuclear facilities during his presidency after US forces struck three sites during the June 2025 war. clusters.headline: Brent oil price passes $90 as Iran-US deal hopes fade

items.title: Brent oil price passes $90 as Iran-US deal hopes fade
items.summary: Brent oil price passes $90 as Iran-US deal hopes fade The price of Brent North Sea crude, the main international oil contract, climbed above $90 on Tuesday as hopes that the US and Iran reach a deal to end the war fade. Brent reached $90.02 a barrel, a gain of more than 2.5 percent from Monday, while the main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, jumped 2.7 percent to $84.32 a barrel. Crude has surged more than 10 percent over the past week, with the US and Iran appearing no closer to a deal on the Strait of Hormuz despite optimistic comments from Washington earlier this month. In the latest blow, Donald Trump said on Monday he would seek conflict compensation from Iran as part of any peace negotiations, responding to Tehran's own demand for US war reparations as a condition of any deal.

clusters.headline: Iran to increase gas production, says state minister

items.title: Iran to increase gas production, says state minister
items.summary: Iran to increase gas production, says state minister Iran will bring back 95 million cubic metres of gas to its production cycle by the end of September, oil minister Mohsen Paknejad said on Tuesday, according to the oil ministry's news outlet, as Tehran conducts repairs on energy infrastructure targeted by Israel and the US. items.title: Saudi Arabia, Yemen condemn attack on UAE oil tanker
items.summary: Saudi Arabia, Yemen condemn attack on UAE oil tanker Saudi Arabia has condemned the attack on an oil tanker operated by the UAE’s ADNOC while transiting the Strait of Hormuz as “an assault on global energy security”. The UAE had blamed Iran for the attack, condemned also by Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar and Syria. In a statement, the Saudi ministry of foreign affairs said: “These reprehensible attacks constitute an assault on the security and safety of maritime navigation, as well as on the security of global energy supplies.” The statement added that the kingdom “holds Iran responsible for the consequences of its continued acts of aggression and calls on Iran to immediately cease these violations”. Yemen’s ministry of foreign affairs joined the condemnation and called the attack “a serious threat to the security and safety of maritime navigation and commercial vessels”.

Saudi Arabia said Iran must immediately cease what it called continued aggression and reaffirmed its support for the United Arab Emirates. Qatar also described the attack as a “flagrant violation” of international law and freedom of navigation. Doha rejected Iran’s use of the Strait of Hormuz as a “bargaining chip” and called for the waterway to be reopened without conditions, warning that its continued closure threatens regional economies and global trade.

items.title: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report
items.summary: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report The US has exhausted its stockpile of sophisticated long-range missiles during the war on Iran, suggesting that there are supply limits to President Donald Trump’s threat to subject the Islamic Republic to the "biggest attack" since World War II. The US has drained its supply of surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing two sources who said the US had used "virtually all" of these munitions. These long-range missiles are a critical part of the US’s arsenal, allowing it to accurately target foes from a distance without relying on warplanes that are vulnerable to air defence systems. Reuters reported that US Central Command - which oversees military operations in the Middle East - has had to replenish its stock of surface-to-surface missiles from other theatres of operation. A years-long truce in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government appeared to collapse last month. items.summary: Pentagon orders arms production surge as Israeli-US war on Iran depletes missiles The Pentagon has ordered US arms manufacturers to accelerate weapons production as the Israeli-US war on Iran depletes American munition stockpiles. In a memo obtained by The Washington Post, Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg gave defence companies 21 days to explain how they would “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities”. “Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.” The order exposes the mounting strain the war has placed on US weapons reserves and follows tensions between President Donald Trump and Pentagon officials over dwindling missile supplies.

He was optimistic about the impact a deal with Iran over the strait would have on energy prices, where he said hundreds of ships are waiting to pass. "Even though things are still a little dicey there over the past few days, we've [seen] quite a few ships coming out even now," Bessent said. "So, you know, I'd expect the energy prices to settle back down, which, as I said, will be good for the entire world."

items.summary: For the first time in years, Washington is discussing Turkey's return to the F-35 program as a serious possibility. At the NATO summit in Ankara last month, President Donald Trump said he would lift the CAATSA sanctions that the U.S. imposed on Turkey after Ankara purchased Russian S-400 missile defense systems in 2019. Trump added that he was “certainly” considering restoring Turkey’s access to the F-35 program, which was also suspended at the time.. Notably, a separate sale of American engines for Turkey's domestic KAAN fighter jet has advanced through congressional review. Ankara is also reportedly exploring the transfer of its S-400 batteries to a Gulf state, a step Washington has demanded for years. But the Russian system is no longer the only source of resistance. items.summary: Les rebelles houthis, soutenus par l'Iran, ont revendiqué des frappes dimanche 9 août en Arabie saoudite contre une raffinerie du géant pétrolier Aramco, puis au Yémen contre le port de Mokha, contrôlé par les forces gouvernementales, internationalement reconnues et soutenues par Riyad. Depuis le mois dernier, les affrontements entre les deux ont repris. Cela fait dire à l'envoyé spécial des Nations unies au Yémen que jamais depuis la trêve conclue en 2022, le risque d'une reprise du conflit n'a été aussi fort.

items.title: Houthi-aanval doodt zeven mensen in Jemen, ook Saudische raffinaderij geraakt
items.summary: Bij een aanval van Houthi's op de Jemenitische havenstad Mokka zijn zeker zeven doden gevallen. Het gaat om vier militairen en drie burgers, melden de Nationale Verzetsstrijdkrachten, die verbonden zijn aan de Jemenitische regering. Minstens vijftien mensen raakten gewond. Onder meer havengebouwen en voedselvoorraden zijn beschadigd geraakt door de raket- en drone-aanvallen. De Houthi's zeggen dat de aanvallen gericht waren tegen militair personeel en opslagplaatsen. Ook een raffinaderij in de Saudische stad Jizan werd getroffen. Het Saudische ministerie van Energie meldde vandaag dat een brand in een installatie van de Aramco-raffinaderij was geblust. Bij de brand vielen geen slachtoffers, aldus het ministerie. Vrijdag voerden Houthi's al aanvallen uit op Jemenitische legerkampen en in Saudi-Arabië. Daarbij kwamen zeker 58 militairen om het leven en raakten meerdere Saudische burgers gewond. items.title: Olieramp voor Omaanse kust: tanker van Russische schaduwvloot al weken gestrand
items.summary: Voor de zuidkust van Oman voltrekt zich een olieramp. Er lekt ruwe aardolie uit een vastgelopen tanker die naar schatting zeker 800.000 vaten vervoert. Op satellietbeelden is te zien dat het schip verder wegzakt onder water, meldt persbureau AP. De tanker is genaamd Caroline Bezengi en maakt volgens Europese landen deel uit van de Russische schaduwvloot waarmee westerse sancties tegen Rusland worden omzeild. Het schip werd begin juni getroffen door een of meerdere explosies. Wat de ontploffingen heeft veroorzaakt, is nog steeds onduidelijk. De tanker ligt inmiddels al anderhalve maand op de rotsen voor het Omaanse eiland Jazirat Al Qibliyyah en heeft daar een kilometerslange olievlek veroorzaakt. Ramp voor lokaal ecosysteem Er zijn grote zorgen over de gevolgen voor het milieu. Op en rondom het eiland komen onder meer zeldzame soorten zeeschildpadden en walvissen voor. "Voor het lokale ecosysteem is het een ramp", zegt milieu- en conflictonderzoeker Wim Zwijnenburg. items.title: President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip | Simon Tisdall
items.summary: Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country Imagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55 ethnic and religious minorities who together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population. Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. items.summary: Pezeshkian says Iran open to dialogue, warns against regional divisions Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian has said Tehran is prepared to pursue dialogue to protect its national interests but will not accept demands that undermine its sovereignty or defensive capabilities, IRNA reported. In an address to the Iranian public, Pezeshkian stressed improved relations with neighbouring countries and the need to prevent regional divisions, the report said. The president rejected claims that his administration had pressured the country’s leadership into accepting negotiations. Pezeshkian stressed that Iran regarded Muslim countries as brothers and questioned why Muslim states should become involved in conflict with one another, IRNA reported. He warned that the US and Israel sought to bring Persian Gulf countries together against Iran, while Tehran worked to prevent it. Tehran would not accept dismantling Iran’s military and defence capabilities, while pursuing dialogue when it protected national interests.

items.summary: US Treasury targets crypto exchanges in new Iran sanctions The United States on Friday sanctioned an unlicensed multi-state cryptocurrency exchange, alleging it processed millions of dollars of crypto for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other groups linked to the Iranian state. The designation follows a Reuters investigation published on 31 July that identified the Dubai-based exchange, Shelbit, as the hub of a $4bn Iranian sanctions evasion scheme. The investigation found that Shelbit, one of the world’s largest illegal online gambling networks, moved crypto on behalf of Iran’s central bank and to addresses linked by the Israeli government to the IRGC. The US Treasury also sanctioned the expatriate Iranian who founded Shelbit and a network of other companies, Siavash Kayvanpour, for providing material support to the IRGC and Nobitex, Iran’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange. items.summary: Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia sign "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement" Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed a defence agreement on Friday, Pakistan's foreign ministry and Saudi broadcasters said. The pact, which was called the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement", ties together the three countries amid the backdrop of war on Iran and a revived conflict with Houthis in Saudi Arabia's southern neighbour Yemen. A Turkish spokesperson said the deal was purely defensive in nature, and not against any actor in particular.

items.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to 'sign defence pact' on Friday
items.summary: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to 'sign defence pact' on Friday Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will sign a joint defence agreement later on Friday, sources in Ankara told Middle East Eye. The deal, which has been under negotiation since last year, marks a significant new trilateral framework amid a deepening regional crisis following Israeli and US attacks on Iran. Saudi analysts have previously said that Riyadh could activate the defence pact it currently has with Pakistan should it enter the Iran war. Friday's proposed deal could have similar implications for Turkey, which is already a US and Nato ally. However, it is not clear what Friday's deal will include in terms of mutual defence. The deal is expected to be signed in Mecca, one of Islam’s holiest sites, by the leaders of the three Muslim-majority countries. clusters.headline: Syria walks a tightrope as war engulfs the Middle East

items.title: Syria walks a tightrope as war engulfs the Middle East
items.summary: Syria has so far avoided becoming a battlefield in the U.S.-Israel-Iran crisis, but it has not escaped the consequences. As regional peace remains elusive, Syria is confronting the challenge of rebuilding following years of gruesome civil war while shielding its fragile recovery from a new wave of geopolitical turmoil. The relatively new Syrian government has prioritized reconstruction, foreign investment, and institution rebuilding. However, the expanding crisis has already created economic and security pressures through trade disruptions, investor uncertainty, and new refugee flows. Higher transportation and insurance costs, along with increased caution among investors, threaten to slow Syria’s recovery just as the country seeks to move beyond its long civil war. Making matters worse is the fact that most Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states’ economies are experiencing contraction as a result of the Iran war, meaning that their earlier economic memoranda of understanding (MoUs) and agreements with Damascus are likely to be cut back, if not eliminated. clusters.headline: The rise or fail of middle powers will determine Middle East peace

items.title: The rise or fail of middle powers will determine Middle East peace
items.summary: For more than two decades, endless wars have destabilized the Middle East, creating huge amounts of human suffering, displacement and trauma. The region is exhausted, with little faith in the possibility of peace and few structures to enable it. The region is now at an inflection point; it can continue endless violence or undertake serious mediation and conflict resolution. The war with Iran has exposed the limits of U.S. military power, leaving only one practical option on the table: pursuing negotiations that recognize the balance of power in the region and the security concerns of all parties. This requires very careful engagement and mediation. There are multiple overlapping conflicts and rivalries within the region. Breaking this cycle requires more than another round of emergency diplomacy; it requires permanent structures for mediation and peacemaking. items.summary: Israel’s Mossad chief fires two senior officials over failure to topple Iran’s leadership Israel’s Mossad chief, Roman Gofman, has sacked two top officials over a failed plan to topple Iran’s government, Israeli media reported. According to Israel’s Channel 12 and Haaretz, one of the officials had served since December as the head of Mossad’s intelligence directorate, while the other was the head of the agency’s Iran division. The reports say the two devised to remove Iran’s leadership by mobilising the country’s minority groups to rebel and whip up mass protests to oust the government - a plan which did not transpire.

clusters.headline: En Iran, «aujourd'hui, on ne sait pas vraiment qui gouverne»

items.title: En Iran, «aujourd'hui, on ne sait pas vraiment qui gouverne»
items.summary: Qui détient aujourd'hui la réalité du pouvoir en Iran ? La question est régulièrement posée, notamment par l'administration Trump. Elle explique ainsi la difficulté à faire avancer les négociations. Il y a d'une part un président et son ministre des Affaires étrangères, qui font partie du camp modéré ; de l'autre, il y a Mojtaba Khamenei, nouveau guide suprême depuis l'assassinat d'Ali Khamenei, au premier jour de la guerre israélo-états-unienne contre l'Iran, le 28 février 2026. Ce dernier est décrit comme tenant d'une ligne dure, proche de l'armée idéologique du régime, les Gardiens de la révolution. Entretien avec Jonathan Piron, historien spécialiste de l'Iran et chercheur associé au Groupe de recherche et d'information sur la paix et la sécurité (GRIP) à Bruxelles.

clusters.headline: Surprise strikes signal Iran is digging in for a long war

items.title: Surprise strikes signal Iran is digging in for a long war
items.summary: In recent weeks, Iran has gone on the offensive, striking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and launching a surprise attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. From a distance, these moves look like self-defeating escalation. Why should a badly damaged state, under severe economic pressure, lash out at the U.S. instead of pushing for a ceasefire? The answer, simply put, is that Iran is digging in for a long war. Whatever Washington's intentions, Tehran increasingly interprets sanctions, negotiations, temporary ceasefires and military strikes as different instruments aimed at a single objective: regime change. As long as this primary objective remains, Iran expects no sanctions relief or meaningful de-escalation. My conversations with Iranian foreign policy analysts suggest that Tehran now believes the war will continue in different forms until the end of Donald Trump's presidency. clusters.headline: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report

items.title: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report
items.summary: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report US President Donald Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Washington's critical shortage of munition during the war on Iran, The Washington Post reported. According to the newspaper citing sources, Trump demanded answers during a cabinet meeting last week after finding out about the deficit in vital weapons, despite his understanding that the issue had been addressed. The report cited the shortage in munitions as one of the reasons behind Trump's decision to pause large-scale strikes against Iran. During the meeting, Hegseth reportedly defended himself and instead blamed Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg for the shortages and "for not ensuring Trump was fully apprised" about the state of Washington's stockpiles. The White House denied the report, with press secretary Karoline Leavitt calling it "100% fake news", adding that Trump saying "has the utmost confidence" in Hegseth.

items.summary: Oorlogsmoe was Amerika, na decennia van 'forever wars', de langdurige strijd van het Amerikaanse leger in andere landen, zoals in Vietnam en Afghanistan. Toch is het de president die beloofde daar een einde aan te maken, die nu de zesde maand ingaat van zijn oorlog met Iran. De onvrede onder Amerikanen groeit. Ook in Middletown, de stad in Ohio waar vicepresident JD Vance werd geboren. "Het stuitert alle kanten op, we hebben geen duidelijk doel", verzucht veteraan John Cox. Hij is gepensioneerd sergeant eerste klasse en diende in Vietnam. "Toen was het idee ook dat we er snel in en ook weer uit zouden gaan." Die oorlog zou uiteindelijk negentien jaar duren. Zo lang loopt de oorlog met Iran nog niet. Maar bij Post 218, een organisatie voor veteranen in Middletown, is er weinig begrip voor de wispelturigheid van Donald Trump. "De ene dag noemt hij het een oorlog, dan weer een schermutseling", zegt Cox aan de bar van Post 218, een soort clubhuis voor veteranen. "Wij horen geen land te zijn dat steeds van koers verandert. Wij moeten ergens naartoe gaan, de klus klaren en weer vertrekken.

clusters.headline: Beyond Hormuz: The Future of Maritime Chokepoints

items.title: Beyond Hormuz: The Future of Maritime Chokepoints
items.summary: Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz and efforts to extract payments for safe passage — plus, more recently, the Houthis’ move to attack Saudi shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — have highlighted the risks of maritime chokepoints to global shipping and raised questions about the future for freedom of navigation. The impacts extend beyond the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, so we asked five experts to consider the implications for several other crucial waterways: the Strait of Malacca, the Taiwan Strait, the Panama Canal, the Suez Canal, and the Turkish Straits.Read more below.Patrick M. CroninAsia-Pacific Security Chair The post Beyond Hormuz: The Future of Maritime Chokepoints appeared first on War on the Rocks .

items.summary: Saudi Aramco reports bumper profits as it bypasses Strait of Hormuz Saudi Aramco said on Tuesday its profits surged 33 percent in the second quarter of this year, as the kingdom benefited from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which drove up energy prices, while its oil pipeline allowed it to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned Saudi Arabian oil giant’s adjusted net income rose to $33.4bn from $25.2bn a year ago. The second quarter runs from early April to the end of June. The US and Iran reached a ceasefire in April that was extended in June, but fighting has continued to rage, keeping energy prices inflated. Iran is attempting to assert its control over the Strait of Hormuz and has attacked dozens of vessels trying to transit the strait via Oman’s territorial waters. The US has bombarded Iran, and in response, Tehran has targeted Gulf states, particularly Kuwait and Bahrain. items.title: Israel-Lebanon negotiations 'stalling': 'Situation on ground far from spirit of framework agreement'
items.summary: Carys Garland is pleased to welcome Joseph BAHOUT, Director, Issam Fares Institute for Public Policy & International Affairs. Despite the symbolism of a seventh round of US-sponsored negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, Bahout argues that the process is increasingly characterised by stagnation rather than diplomatic momentum. He suggests that the core obstacles are no longer merely technical disagreements over the implementation of the June framework agreement, but a convergence of military realities, domestic political constraints, diminishing American engagement, and wider regional tensions. The negotiations, in his view, exist within a broader strategic ecosystem in which progress on Lebanese-Israeli arrangements remains contingent upon developments in the Iran-US war and Israeli domestic politics.

items.title: Robert Kagan: Sometimes US intervention is worth blowback
items.summary: Robert Kagan surprised some people. One of America’s most influential hawks condemned the Trump administration’s botched war in Iran, suggesting in The Atlantic in March that U.S. involvement in the Middle East has been a catalyst of, rather than a prudent response to, Islamic terrorism. A senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and prolific historian, Kagan has advocated U.S. primacy for decades, starting with his support for Nicaragua’s Contra insurgents as the head of the State Department’s Office of Public Diplomacy (1985-88). In 1997, Kagan co-founded Project for the New American Century, a neoconservative think tank that lobbied for a muscular foreign policy and the maintenance of U.S. global hegemony. The group exercised its considerable influence to push regime change in Saddam Hussein’s Iraq. Kagan’s advocacy has always been based on a belief that the world would collapse into disorder without American leadership, even though U.S. military misadventures have repeatedly destabilized parts of the world. But for many senators, the top priority is not enacting legislation that will help Americans but instead rushing to approve the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 , known colloquially as the “Russia sanctions bill.” A passion project of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the bill is intended to increase economic pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin. The legislation’s backers hope that, by choking off funding for Russia’s war effort, they can force Moscow to make greater concessions in ongoing negotiations to end the four-year old conflict in Ukraine. But this logic and the bill itself are fundamentally flawed. The new legislation will have a limited effect on Russia’s fortunes; as has been the case since the beginning of the war, additional economic punishments are unlikely to be decisive in Putin’s calculus. items.summary: Report: Pentagon is emailing military experts and asking best way to 'punish' Iran The Trump administration seems to be struggling to figure out how to get out of its self-made Iran quagmire. According to a CNN report on Monday, the US military is now crowdsourcing ideas among military experts for what to do next in order to push Iran into a deal that is to President Donald Trump's liking. "We are looking for new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran," an email from an officer in US Central Command's (Centcom) intelligence branch read last week, according to the CNN report. A Centcom spokesperson said the move is not unusual, and that it "has a long history of thinking and working in innovative ways". But the email suggests the Pentagon did not plan for the conflict to drag out this long. Read more: Pentagon is emailing military experts and asking best way to 'punish' Iran: Report

His comments were a reference to the support Iran lent Kuwait during the Gulf War (1990-91), and were made as American military bases in Kuwait came under fire by Iranian missiles. items.summary: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history It’s five years this month since the chaotic retreat of US forces from Kabul. The Nato-backed invasion and occupation of Afghanistan, launched after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC, is now widely regarded as a failure. It cost the lives of more than 2,400 US and 450 British troops, and tens of thousands of civilians (the exact number is unknown). Although al-Qaida terrorists were routed, their Taliban hosts reimposed repressive, misogynistic Islamist rule after regaining power in 2021. Afghanistan became a byword for ill-considered western interventionism and nation-building. It was the archetypal “forever war”, a phrase first coined during Vietnam . If this cautionary tale had any lasting value, it was as a deterrent to politicians and generals tempted to rashly embark on open-ended conflicts without just cause, defined, achievable aims, and an exit strategy. In an interview with Channel 12, Bennett described Qatar as “more dangerous” to Israel at the moment than Iran. “With Iran, everyone knows that [it says], ‘We’ll destroy Israel.’” But Qatar, he said, “funded the Nukhba terrorists of October 7 [2023]… Qatar operates Al Jazeera, which is the most poisonous cancer hurting us.” “Qatar reaches places of influence in American universities… And most importantly, [it has access] to the most sacred place for the security of Israel — that is the office of the prime minister of Israel,” he said. "Qatar works against us and poisons us from within,” Bennett said, fuming that Israel does not define Qatar as an enemy state.

clusters.headline: Pezeshkian recalls Haniyeh assassination, hails Iranians as 'real heroes'

items.title: Pezeshkian recalls Haniyeh assassination, hails Iranians as 'real heroes'
items.summary: Pezeshkian recalls Haniyeh assassination, hails Iranians as 'real heroes' Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian marked two years in office by recalling the killing of Hamas political chief Ismail Haniyeh and praising the Iranian people's resilience through “relentless hostility”. In a statement carried by IRNA, Pezeshkian said his presidency began under the shadow of tragedy, noting that "the beginning of my administration coincided with the assassination of our dear guest by the Zionist regime." Haniyeh was assassinated in Tehran on 31 July 2024, hours after attending Pezeshkian's inauguration, where delegations from more than 70 countries were present. Pezeshkian's presidency has since been marked by what he called "wars, pressure, and relentless hostility" against Iran, including a foreign-backed coup attempt and two US-Israeli wars. "Throughout all these difficult days, the real heroes were the people," he said, adding that Iranians "will shape the future of Iran."

items.title: Rubio says Iran confronting 'different kind of US president' under Trump
items.summary: Rubio says Iran confronting 'different kind of US president' under Trump US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has said Iran was confronting a different kind of US president under  Donald Trump, adding Tehran can no longer rely on negotiations without consequences. In an interview with Fox News, Rubio said: “I don’t think the Iranian regime has ever faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action.” “They got used to, for 20 or 30 years, not just the US, but the broader world, allowing them to get away with things like lying, breaking deals, tricking people into agreements.” The comments come as Trump warned on Friday that he will hit Iran "very hard" amid reports that he was considering renewed heavy attacks as soon as this weekend, including against Iran's energy infrastructure targets.

items.title: IRGC says three F-35 fighters destroyed at Jordan's Al-Azraq Base
items.summary: IRGC says three F-35 fighters destroyed at Jordan's Al-Azraq Base Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that its Aerospace Force targeted the US F-35 repair hangar and ramp at Al-Azraq Base in Jordan with multiple ballistic missiles on Sunday morning, IRNA reported. The IRGC said that the attack, in which it claimed to have destroyed three F-35 fighters and damaged three others, avenged "the American aggression on Qeshm Island". Iranian authorities said that a couple and their two-year-old child were killed and two other children were injured in an American strike on a building on Qeshm Island on 30 July. The strikes caused widespread damage to property.

items.title: US embassies tell citizens to 'consider departing' Middle East
items.summary: US embassies tell citizens to 'consider departing' Middle East US embassies across the Middle East have issued security alerts urging American citizens to "consider departing" the region due to "the potential for an unforseen escalation" in the conflict between the US and Iran. The warnings come after US President Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran "very hard" on Friday amid widespread US media reports anticipating an escalation in US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure. "Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions," said an alert circulated by the US embassy in Jordan, with versions of the same text also posted by the American missions in Jerusalem, Muscat, Baghdad and Beirut. Americans in Jordan were also advised to avoid travel to military bases in the country and to "exercise caution and stay alert at locations publicly associated with the United States."

items.title: Brent oil price passes $90 as Iran-US deal hopes fade
items.summary: Brent oil price passes $90 as Iran-US deal hopes fade The price of Brent North Sea crude, the main international oil contract, climbed above $90 on Tuesday as hopes that the US and Iran reach a deal to end the war fade. Brent reached $90.02 a barrel, a gain of more than 2.5 percent from Monday, while the main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, jumped 2.7 percent to $84.32 a barrel. Crude has surged more than 10 percent over the past week, with the US and Iran appearing no closer to a deal on the Strait of Hormuz despite optimistic comments from Washington earlier this month. In the latest blow, Donald Trump said on Monday he would seek conflict compensation from Iran as part of any peace negotiations, responding to Tehran's own demand for US war reparations as a condition of any deal.

items.summary: Iran supreme leader names IRGC General Abdollahi military chief Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei named Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps General Ali Abdollahi head of the country's armed forces on Monday, while also confirming a new commander of the Guard, putting his imprimatur on the country's military. Abdollahi had previously led the Khatam al-Anbiya, Iran's inter-branch central military command tasked with coordinating operations. A statement on Khamenei's website announced that "Major General Ali Abdollahi has been appointed chief of staff of the armed forces. Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi has also been appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps with the rank of major general." The pair represent Khamenei's first senior military appointments since being named supreme leader early in the Middle East war after the death of his father in US-Israeli strikes.

items.title: Why the Trump administration will have to accept a Hormuz toll
items.summary: In the weeks since the U.S.-Iran Memorandum of Understanding collapsed, Washington and Tehran have used the time to strengthen their respective positions in the event negotiations resume. For the United States, this has largely taken the form of overt threats by President Donald Trump himself and hints that an even more comprehensive U.S. bombing campaign against Iranian strategic targets is on the table. For Iran, the strategy is familiar: ensure maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is kept to an absolute minimum . U.S. and Iranian officials continue to give conflicting accounts of where negotiations stand. Despite Trump’s repeated declarations that Tehran is begging for a deal, the Iranians stress no talks are occurring with the United States. Still, both sides seem to agree that any pending agreement will center on the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has proved capable of shutting down at will. items.title: Israel is going all out to stop Turkey from getting F-35s
items.summary: For the first time in years, Washington is discussing Turkey's return to the F-35 program as a serious possibility. At the NATO summit in Ankara last month, President Donald Trump said he would lift the CAATSA sanctions that the U.S. imposed on Turkey after Ankara purchased Russian S-400 missile defense systems in 2019. Trump added that he was “certainly” considering restoring Turkey’s access to the F-35 program, which was also suspended at the time.. Notably, a separate sale of American engines for Turkey's domestic KAAN fighter jet has advanced through congressional review. Ankara is also reportedly exploring the transfer of its S-400 batteries to a Gulf state, a step Washington has demanded for years. But the Russian system is no longer the only source of resistance. Israel argues that Turkish F-35s would, in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's words, " destroy the power balance " in the region. items.title: Iran appoints former IRGC chief to top security post
items.summary: Iran appoints former IRGC chief to top security post Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has named former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Mohsen Rezaee as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Rezaee will also serve as Khamenei’s representative on the council, placing him at the centre of Iran’s security and defence decision-making. He succeeds Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who took over the position after US-Israeli attacks assassinated Ali Larijani in March. Rezaee previously commanded the IRGC and currently sits on Iran’s Expediency Discernment Council. The body mediates disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council, which reviews legislation and vets candidates seeking public office. The veteran commander played a leading military role during the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s. Khamenei appointed Zolghadr as his political adviser as part of the leadership reshuffle. items.title: Trump says US is ‘only semi-negotiating’ with Iran
items.summary: Trump says US is ‘only semi-negotiating’ with Iran US President Donald Trump says Washington is “only semi-negotiating” with Iran. Trump speaking to Axios claimed that Iran was in “very bad shape”, pointing to soaring inflation and “the fact they have no money”. He said Tehran could not afford to pay its soldiers and credited the US naval blockade with worsening its financial troubles. Trump made no mention of the war’s economic toll on the US. Higher fuel prices have cost ordinary Americans about $80bn, while military operations have cost more than $100bn. “It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game,” Trump said. “We are low-keying it.”

items.title: Middle East crisis live: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Gaza plan and vows no withdrawal until Hamas disarms

items.summary: Pentagon orders arms production surge as Israeli-US war on Iran depletes missiles The Pentagon has ordered US arms manufacturers to accelerate weapons production as the Israeli-US war on Iran depletes American munition stockpiles. In a memo obtained by The Washington Post, Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg gave defence companies 21 days to explain how they would “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities”. “Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.” The order exposes the mounting strain the war has placed on US weapons reserves and follows tensions between President Donald Trump and Pentagon officials over dwindling missile supplies.

items.summary: Iran sets conditions for reopening Strait of Hormuz Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has outlined Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB, Zolghadr said Washington must “correct its behaviour” by: Ending threats against Iran and its “sacred values” Permanently halting military action against Iran and its regional allies Withdrawing US naval and air forces involved in the blockade of Iran Compensating Iran for damage inflicted during the recent conflict Lifting US sanctions Releasing frozen Iranian assets “The Supreme National Security Council will not retreat from these demands, whether in war or in negotiations,” Zolghadr said.

items.title: Turkey says Saudi-Pakistan defence pact mirrors NATO’s Article 5, Egypt could also join
items.summary: Turkey says Saudi-Pakistan defence pact mirrors NATO’s Article 5, Egypt could also join Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan says the new defence agreement between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia is technically equivalent to NATO’s Article 5 mutual defence clause and does not target Iran. Fidan told Turkey’s Anadolu news agency that the three countries would establish a ministerial committee resembling NATO’s decision-making structure. The pact will also have a general secretariat based in Saudi Arabia. Egypt could join the alliance once the parties resolve outstanding technical issues, Fidan added. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the agreement on Friday.

items.title: President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip | Simon Tisdall
items.summary: Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country Imagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55 ethnic and religious minorities who together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population. Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. In an address to the Iranian public, Pezeshkian stressed improved relations with neighbouring countries and the need to prevent regional divisions, the report said. The president rejected claims that his administration had pressured the country’s leadership into accepting negotiations. Pezeshkian stressed that Iran regarded Muslim countries as brothers and questioned why Muslim states should become involved in conflict with one another, IRNA reported. He warned that the US and Israel sought to bring Persian Gulf countries together against Iran, while Tehran worked to prevent it. Tehran would not accept dismantling Iran’s military and defence capabilities, while pursuing dialogue when it protected national interests.

items.title: US Treasury targets crypto exchanges in new Iran sanctions
items.summary: US Treasury targets crypto exchanges in new Iran sanctions The United States on Friday sanctioned an unlicensed multi-state cryptocurrency exchange, alleging it processed millions of dollars of crypto for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other groups linked to the Iranian state. The designation follows a Reuters investigation published on 31 July that identified the Dubai-based exchange, Shelbit, as the hub of a $4bn Iranian sanctions evasion scheme. The investigation found that Shelbit, one of the world’s largest illegal online gambling networks, moved crypto on behalf of Iran’s central bank and to addresses linked by the Israeli government to the IRGC. The US Treasury also sanctioned the expatriate Iranian who founded Shelbit and a network of other companies, Siavash Kayvanpour, for providing material support to the IRGC and Nobitex, Iran’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange. items.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to 'sign defence pact' on Friday
items.summary: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to 'sign defence pact' on Friday Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will sign a joint defence agreement later on Friday, sources in Ankara told Middle East Eye. The deal, which has been under negotiation since last year, marks a significant new trilateral framework amid a deepening regional crisis following Israeli and US attacks on Iran. Saudi analysts have previously said that Riyadh could activate the defence pact it currently has with Pakistan should it enter the Iran war. Friday's proposed deal could have similar implications for Turkey, which is already a US and Nato ally. However, it is not clear what Friday's deal will include in terms of mutual defence. The deal is expected to be signed in Mecca, one of Islam’s holiest sites, by the leaders of the three Muslim-majority countries. items.title: Syria walks a tightrope as war engulfs the Middle East
items.summary: Syria has so far avoided becoming a battlefield in the U.S.-Israel-Iran crisis, but it has not escaped the consequences. As regional peace remains elusive, Syria is confronting the challenge of rebuilding following years of gruesome civil war while shielding its fragile recovery from a new wave of geopolitical turmoil. The relatively new Syrian government has prioritized reconstruction, foreign investment, and institution rebuilding. However, the expanding crisis has already created economic and security pressures through trade disruptions, investor uncertainty, and new refugee flows. Higher transportation and insurance costs, along with increased caution among investors, threaten to slow Syria’s recovery just as the country seeks to move beyond its long civil war. Making matters worse is the fact that most Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states’ economies are experiencing contraction as a result of the Iran war, meaning that their earlier economic memoranda of understanding (MoUs) and agreements with Damascus are likely to be cut back, if not eliminated. items.title: The rise or fail of middle powers will determine Middle East peace
items.summary: For more than two decades, endless wars have destabilized the Middle East, creating huge amounts of human suffering, displacement and trauma. The region is exhausted, with little faith in the possibility of peace and few structures to enable it. The region is now at an inflection point; it can continue endless violence or undertake serious mediation and conflict resolution. The war with Iran has exposed the limits of U.S. military power, leaving only one practical option on the table: pursuing negotiations that recognize the balance of power in the region and the security concerns of all parties. This requires very careful engagement and mediation. There are multiple overlapping conflicts and rivalries within the region. Breaking this cycle requires more than another round of emergency diplomacy; it requires permanent structures for mediation and peacemaking. Elle explique ainsi la difficulté à faire avancer les négociations. Il y a d'une part un président et son ministre des Affaires étrangères, qui font partie du camp modéré ; de l'autre, il y a Mojtaba Khamenei, nouveau guide suprême depuis l'assassinat d'Ali Khamenei, au premier jour de la guerre israélo-états-unienne contre l'Iran, le 28 février 2026. Ce dernier est décrit comme tenant d'une ligne dure, proche de l'armée idéologique du régime, les Gardiens de la révolution. Entretien avec Jonathan Piron, historien spécialiste de l'Iran et chercheur associé au Groupe de recherche et d'information sur la paix et la sécurité (GRIP) à Bruxelles.

According to the report, senior US military officials warned that the Pentagon’s munitions stockpile is "dangerously low," with key air defence systems particularly depleted during the war on Iran. The US military exhausted nearly four-fifths of its THAAD missile inventory compared to pre-war figures. Meanwhile, half of its Patriot interceptors were burned through since the start of the war. One source familiar with recent internal Pentagon reports noted that the army used "virtually all" of its highly accurate long-range, surface-to-air weapons in the same period.

items.title: Surprise strikes signal Iran is digging in for a long war
items.summary: In recent weeks, Iran has gone on the offensive, striking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and launching a surprise attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. From a distance, these moves look like self-defeating escalation. Why should a badly damaged state, under severe economic pressure, lash out at the U.S. instead of pushing for a ceasefire? The answer, simply put, is that Iran is digging in for a long war. Whatever Washington's intentions, Tehran increasingly interprets sanctions, negotiations, temporary ceasefires and military strikes as different instruments aimed at a single objective: regime change. As long as this primary objective remains, Iran expects no sanctions relief or meaningful de-escalation. My conversations with Iranian foreign policy analysts suggest that Tehran now believes the war will continue in different forms until the end of Donald Trump's presidency. There is no doubt that the war has punished Iran’s economy. items.title: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report
items.summary: Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report US President Donald Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Washington's critical shortage of munition during the war on Iran, The Washington Post reported. According to the newspaper citing sources, Trump demanded answers during a cabinet meeting last week after finding out about the deficit in vital weapons, despite his understanding that the issue had been addressed. The report cited the shortage in munitions as one of the reasons behind Trump's decision to pause large-scale strikes against Iran. During the meeting, Hegseth reportedly defended himself and instead blamed Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg for the shortages and "for not ensuring Trump was fully apprised" about the state of Washington's stockpiles. The White House denied the report, with press secretary Karoline Leavitt calling it "100% fake news", adding that Trump saying "has the utmost confidence" in Hegseth.

Zo lang loopt de oorlog met Iran nog niet. Maar bij Post 218, een organisatie voor veteranen in Middletown, is er weinig begrip voor de wispelturigheid van Donald Trump. "De ene dag noemt hij het een oorlog, dan weer een schermutseling", zegt Cox aan de bar van Post 218, een soort clubhuis voor veteranen. "Wij horen geen land te zijn dat steeds van koers verandert. The cultural and political contexts in which the arms control and disarmament movement exists have changed dramatically over the past decade, and our methods for connecting with the younger members of the public must keep pace to remain effective. Sadly, there’s no magic formula for navigating these changes perfectly. items.title: Afternoon update
items.summary: Afternoon update Good afternoon Middle East Eye readers, Here are the latest developments from across the region: Israel has conducted a drone strike in southern Lebanon, killing one and injuring 11, Lebanese media reports. The strike targeted a prayer area in a cemetery, and caused a fire and explosion. This came shortly after an Israeli warning ordering residents to leave their homes. The Israeli army said the strikes were in response to what it described as a "violation of the ceasefire" by Hezbollah, despite ongoing US-sponsored negotiations between Israel and Lebanon in Rome. Iranian sources say a deal with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz is close to concluding, which would give Tehran control over the inbound route and Muscat partial control over the outbound one. Iran says the deal would not lead to an immediate reopening of the strait, and that US President Trump's threats are currently the biggest obstacle to the conclusion of the negotiations. items.title: Will Trump meet his Suez moment & seize Hormuz deal on the table?
items.summary: Oman and Iran appear close to a temporary arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, potentially providing both an exit from the current round of fighting and the foundation for a more durable maritime order. Washington should welcome such an agreement—even if it acknowledges a degree of Iranian authority in administering traffic through the strait—because US interest dictates that open and non-discriminatory passage must be given priority over control. The emerging formula would reportedly divide responsibility for the shipping lanes. Vessels entering the Persian Gulf would travel through waters administered by Iran, while outbound traffic would pass through an Omani-administered route. Iran would be notified of departing vessels and, while this has not yet been discussed, Tehran appears open to also ensuring that Oman would be notified of incoming traffic. Tehran and Muscat may collect and share fees for specified security and environmental services, although this sensitive issue has not yet been settled. items.title: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report
items.summary: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report The US has exhausted its stockpile of sophisticated long-range missiles during the war on Iran, suggesting that there are supply limits to President Donald Trump’s threat to subject the Islamic Republic to the "biggest attack" since World War II. The US has drained its supply of surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing two sources who said the US had used "virtually all" of these munitions. These long-range missiles are a critical part of the US’s arsenal, allowing it to accurately target foes from a distance without relying on warplanes that are vulnerable to air defence systems. Reuters reported that US Central Command - which oversees military operations in the Middle East - has had to replenish its stock of surface-to-surface missiles from other theatres of operation. Despite the symbolism of a seventh round of US-sponsored negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, Bahout argues that the process is increasingly characterised by stagnation rather than diplomatic momentum. He suggests that the core obstacles are no longer merely technical disagreements over the implementation of the June framework agreement, but a convergence of military realities, domestic political constraints, diminishing American engagement, and wider regional tensions. items.title: Oil prices fall amid hopes of US-Iran deal
items.summary: Oil prices fall amid hopes of US-Iran deal Oil prices plunged after Qatar said US-Iran negotiations had resumed, and the US treasury secretary suggested a deal could happen "today or tomorrow". These announcements eased concerns over crude supply disruptions that had sent prices soaring in recent months. The main US oil contract, West Texas Intermediate, dropped five percent to $76.32 a barrel, while the international benchmark Brent North Sea crude fell back below $80 a barrel. US stocks have also performed well since the market opened this morning, with the Dow Jones up 1.3 percent, and the S&P 500 hitting an interday record for the first time since June.

items.title: US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles during Iran war, say sources
items.summary: US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles during Iran war, say sources The US army has used up much of its stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles during its five-month war on Iran, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. The US has used "virtually all" munitions for surface-to-surface weapons (ATACMS), and around half of its global Tomahawk supply, the sources said. ATACMS are crucial to allow accurate strikes from a safe distance, and have been widely used by Ukraine against Russia. A person with knowledge of the data said the US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, had burned through nearly all the land-based missiles it had before the war began, and had to resupply from other areas of the world.

items.title: US treasury secretary says Hormuz deal with Iran could happen 'today or tomorrow'
items.summary: US treasury secretary says Hormuz deal with Iran could happen 'today or tomorrow' Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the US could reach a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by Wednesday, adding that this would stabilise energy prices. "We are in talks with the Iranians, and I think there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised position in this conflict," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC. He was optimistic about the impact a deal with Iran over the strait would have on energy prices, where he said hundreds of ships are waiting to pass. "Even though things are still a little dicey there over the past few days, we've [seen] quite a few ships coming out even now," Bessent said. "So, you know, I'd expect the energy prices to settle back down, which, as I said, will be good for the entire world."

A senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and prolific historian, Kagan has advocated U.S. primacy for decades, starting with his support for Nicaragua’s Contra insurgents as the head of the State Department’s Office of Public Diplomacy (1985-88). In 1997, Kagan co-founded Project for the New American Century, a neoconservative think tank that lobbied for a muscular foreign policy and the maintenance of U.S. global hegemony. The group exercised its considerable influence to push regime change in Saddam Hussein’s Iraq. items.summary: As the Senate returns to Washington for its last week in session until mid-September, it faces a long to-do list. But for many senators, the top priority is not enacting legislation that will help Americans but instead rushing to approve the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 , known colloquially as the “Russia sanctions bill.” A passion project of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the bill is intended to increase economic pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin. The legislation’s backers hope that, by choking off funding for Russia’s war effort, they can force Moscow to make greater concessions in ongoing negotiations to end the four-year old conflict in Ukraine. The new legislation will have a limited effect on Russia’s fortunes; as has been the case since the beginning of the war, additional economic punishments are unlikely to be decisive in Putin’s calculus. This comes after Iran denied any talks were ongoing with the US despite Trump’s announcement that negotiations would begin after he decided to cancel strikes against the country. “Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished,” Trump wrote in a post to Truth Social on Monday. “Whether Iran wants to admit it or not, we are, in fact, talking of a solution to a problem that they have caused, for decades. It is very simple, IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!” he added.

items.summary: Oil prices drop following Trump announcement on Iran talks Crude oil futures fell over six percent after President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran would begin imminently to end the war, although Iran denies any such talks are taking place. The drop in oil prices boosted US stocks at the opening, with Dow Jones jumping 1.3 percent, Nasdaq up 1.2 percent, and the broader S&P 500 up 0.9 percent. Trump said he called off what would have been "massive strikes" at the request of Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Brent crude prices dropped five percent to $83.53 a barrel on Monday.

Trump had announced that negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on new strikes against the Islamic Republic in order to pursue a deal. "Obviously, they don't want to be attacked," Trump told reporters on Sunday on board Air Force One. "Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon." However, Iran's foreign ministry has said there were currently no negotiations with the US but that talks were taking place with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthi regime in Yemen, as a direct outgrowth of the U.S.-Iran war, has renewed attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. items.title: Fox News screaming desperately into wind as Trump loses grip
items.summary: Fox News has always served as a purveyor of Republican war propaganda, but its coverage of the Iran conflict has been particularly aggressive, and in many ways unmoored from reality, giving their viewers a more than skewed vision of what President Donald Trump can — and cannot — accomplish in Iran today. It appears that it has been an editorial decision at Fox to convince their audience (whose median age is 55) that the Iranians cannot be negotiated with nor trusted and that war was — and still is — the only option. Its range of hosts and guests continue to insist that Trump’s military campaign has been a rousing success (by all independent, observable accounts it has not) and he just needs to finish the job. It follows a phone call with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who reportedly urged de-escalation, amid fears that Iran could retaliate against the Kingdom and other Gulf states. items.summary: The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history It’s five years this month since the chaotic retreat of US forces from Kabul. The Nato-backed invasion and occupation of Afghanistan, launched after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC, is now widely regarded as a failure. It cost the lives of more than 2,400 US and 450 British troops, and tens of thousands of civilians (the exact number is unknown). Although al-Qaida terrorists were routed, their Taliban hosts reimposed repressive, misogynistic Islamist rule after regaining power in 2021. Afghanistan became a byword for ill-considered western interventionism and nation-building. It was the archetypal “forever war”, a phrase first coined during Vietnam . If this cautionary tale had any lasting value, it was as a deterrent to politicians and generals tempted to rashly embark on open-ended conflicts without just cause, defined, achievable aims, and an exit strategy. items.summary: US embassies tell citizens to 'consider departing' Middle East US embassies across the Middle East have issued security alerts urging American citizens to "consider departing" the region due to "the potential for an unforseen escalation" in the conflict between the US and Iran. The warnings come after US President Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran "very hard" on Friday amid widespread US media reports anticipating an escalation in US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure. "Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions," said an alert circulated by the US embassy in Jordan, with versions of the same text also posted by the American missions in Jerusalem, Muscat, Baghdad and Beirut. Americans in Jordan were also advised to avoid travel to military bases in the country and to "exercise caution and stay alert at locations publicly associated with the United States."

items.title: GCC condemns Iranian attacks in Kuwait
items.summary: GCC condemns Iranian attacks in Kuwait The secretary general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, has criticised Iran, accusing it of attacking civilian facilities in Kuwait. Albudaiwi said Iran targeted a government facility and vehicles belonging to a private company. He argued that these attacks represent "a continuation of its hostile approach to destabilising security and stability in the region". He described them as a "blatant aggression and flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the State of Kuwait" and a "direct threat to its security, stability and the safety of its citizens and residents".

items.summary: Посольства США в Израиле и других странах Ближнего Востока призывают своих граждан быть готовыми к отъезду на фоне напряженности с Ираном."Посольства США в Иерусалиме и других ближневосточных столицах призывают американских граждан на Ближнем Востоке избегать поездок по региону и быть готовыми к отъезду из-за потенциала непредвиденной эскалации" в конфликте с Ираном", - сообщает в субботу Times of Israel."В связи с повышенной напряженностью на Ближнем Востоке обстановка в сфере безопасности остается сложной, с потенциалом непредвиденной эскалации", - говорится в сообщении американских дипмиссий, опубликованном сразу в нескольких регионах.
